text: Sheila Levrant de Bretteville, born in 1940 in Brooklyn, New York, is an American graphic designer, artist, and educator whose work emphasizes feminist principles and user participation in design. Her parents were Polish immigrants who fled anti-semitism in the 1920s and worked in the textile and millinery industries; her mother introduced her to painting lessons at the Brooklyn Museum as a child. She graduated from Abraham Lincoln High School in 1959, where she studied under Leon Friend, who introduced her to modern graphic design and its social responsibilities and encouraged her to enter design and painting competitions. De Bretteville earned a BA in art history from Barnard College in 1962 and an MFA in graphic design from Yale University in 1964. She has received honorary doctorates from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts), the Moore College of Art, and the California College of the Arts. In 1969, she moved to Los Angeles, working as an in-house graphic designer at CalArts before becoming the first woman faculty member in its design department in 1970. In 1971, she founded the first design program for women at CalArts, and two years later co-founded the Woman's Building, a public center in Los Angeles focused on women's education and culture. In 1973, she founded the Women's Graphic Center and co-founded the Feminist Studio Workshop with Judy Chicago and Arlene Raven, both based at the Woman's Building. She designed a necklace featuring an eye bolt on a chain, symbolizing "strength without a fist" and the biological identity of women; she gave the first to Arlene Raven and Judy Chicago when they started the Feminist Studio Workshop in 1972 and has since given similar necklaces to other women aligned with her vision for women's culture. Members of the Feminist Studio Workshop from 1978–79 produced 500 such necklaces to celebrate the fifth anniversary of the Woman's Building. The feminist art group Sisters of Jam (Mikaela & Moa Krestesen) transformed the necklace into a mobile monument, interpreting the eye bolt as a symbol of completed and ongoing work, and installed "Hello Sheila" at the Survival Kit Festival in Umeå in 2014. In 1980, she initiated the communication design program at the Otis College of Art and Design, a division of the New School. De Bretteville has long advocated for communal forms of art as central to the U.S. feminist art movement; in 1973, she created "Pink," a broadside exploring gender and the color pink for an American Institute of Graphic Arts exhibition, which was the only entry on that color. She arranged paper squares into a "quilt" from which posters were printed and distributed in Los Angeles, earning her the nickname "Pinky." She has created numerous public artworks embedded in city neighborhoods, including "Biddy Mason's Place: A Passage of Time," an 82-foot concrete wall with embedded objects in downtown Los Angeles that chronicles the life of Biddy Mason, a former slave who became a midwife in Los Angeles and lived near the site, which she created in collaboration with Betye Saar. In 1994, she completed "Path of Stars" in a New Haven neighborhood, featuring 21 granite stars embedded in the sidewalk documenting the lives of local residents—past and present. In 1996, she collaborated with artist Sonya Ishii on "Remembering Little Tokyo" in Los Angeles, where they interviewed residents and created brass tiles etched with symbols representing local history and Japanese American identities. She also designed the mural "At the Start... At Long Last" for the Inwood-207th Street station in New York City, inspired by the song "Take the A Train" by Billy Strayhorn. De Bretteville was interviewed for the film !Women Art Revolution and is a member of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences. She has received numerous awards, including a 2009 "Grandmaster" award from the New York Art Directors Club, a "Design Legend Gold Medal" from the American Institute of Graphic Arts in 2004, a "Best Public Artwork" recognition from Americans for the Arts in 2005, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Women's Caucus for Art in 2016. In 1990, she became the director of the Yale University Graduate Program in Graphic Design and the first woman to receive tenure at the Yale University School of Art. In 2010, she was named the Caroline M. Street Professor of Graphic Design.
